entry.title: Hot Stove Edition — the Seventeenth of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? Not yet — 94 days until the first spring-training game.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 132 · Tuesday, the Seventeenth of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

No contests this day; the hot stove burns bright.

94 days until the first spring-training game (Friday, the 19th of February, 2027).

News Around the League

THE COOPERSTOWN DESK: SEVEN-AND-TWENTY NAMES GO TO THE WRITERS — POSEY AND LESTER HEAD FOURTEEN NEWCOMERS ON THE BALLOT FOR 2027, UTLEY LEADS THE RETURNING CLASS FROM JUST SHY OF SIXTY PERCENT, AND THE ENVELOPE IS APPOINTED FOR THE NINETEENTH OF JANUARY

The writers have been handed their examination paper. The Baseball Writers' Association unveiled its Hall of Fame ballot for 2027 on Monday — 27 names in all, 14 of them standing before the electorate for the first time — and Cooperstown thus has both of its winter questions on the table at once, for the reader will recall from Sunday's columns that a committee of sixteen already weighs eight managers and executives toward a December 6 verdict. The writers' timetable is longer: ballots must be cast by December 31, three-quarters of them spell election, and the results are to be announced on January 19 at 6 o'clock in the evening, with induction at Cooperstown next July 25 — a date the almanac at Baseball-Reference already carries.231

The newcomers are headed by a catcher with little left to prove. Buster Posey of the Giants was Rookie of the Year in 2010, Most Valuable in 2012 — when his .336 average made him the first National League catcher to win a batting title in 70 years — and a champion three times over, in 2010, 2012 and 2014; he batted .302 across twelve seasons with a 129 OPS+ that ties Mickey Cochrane for fourth among catchers of at least a thousand games, and he walked away in 2021 fresh from a .304 season for a Bay nine that won 107 games, retiring at the very top of his powers. Beside him stands Jon Lester, who beat lymphoma in 2007 and threw a no-hitter the following May, and who closed his books at 200 wins, 2,488 strikeouts and three rings — in the Modern Era, only Spahn, Johnson, Glavine and Kershaw among left-handers have matched that ledger of wins, innings and strikeouts at his quality. The supporting bill runs from Brett Gardner, whose 274 stolen bases as a Yankee trail only Jeter and Henderson in that club's books, to Ryan Zimmerman, Mr. National himself and author of 11 walk-off home runs, to Kyle Seager, a Mariner his whole career and nicknamed, with fraternal cruelty, "Corey's Brother."23

Among the holdovers the arithmetic favors Chase Utley, the only returning man above fifty percent: his support leapt 19.3 points last cycle to 59.1, and another such leap elects him. Andy Pettitte stands at 48.5 in his ninth year of ten; Félix Hernández more than doubled his backing in year two, to 46.1; Alex Rodriguez holds at 40; and Omar Vizquel, at 18.4, faces his tenth and final ballot. The Herald will keep the ledger open through the winter.3

THE SKUBAL REGISTER: THE METROPOLITANS COME CALLING IN PERSON — THE FLUSHING NINE HOLD THEIR FIRST AUDIENCE WITH THE WINTER'S PRIZE ARM IN CALIFORNIA, THE WIRE ALREADY CALLS QUEENS HIS EXPECTED DESTINATION, AND THE ASKING TERMS MAY RUN TO TEN YEARS

The courtship of Tarik Skubal has moved from the telephone to the parlor. On Monday the Mets made their first pitch to the two-time Cy Young laureate in person, sitting down with him in Orange County, California — so reports the insider Jon Heyman in the New York Post, by way of the wire's running register on the man.4 The development surprises no one who has read these columns since Las Vegas: the widespread expectation coming out of the general managers' meetings, as the wire's Mark Feinsand reported it, is that Skubal ends up in Queens, one National League executive putting it baldly — "I don't know who else is really even in the conversation."4

The conversation nonetheless has other voices. The Angelenos, who paid three prospects to rent the left-hander at the summer's trade deadline, remain in it, with the Jays and the Mission nine besides — the reader will recall from Sunday's columns that San Diego has a sitting of its own booked. But the shape of the asking favors the deepest purse and the longest patience: Skubal, 29, seeks a long engagement, the figure mentioned running to somewhere between seven and ten years, and both records on the pitchers' ledger — Yamamoto's twelve-year, $325 million guarantee, and the $43.33 million annual wage shared by Scherzer and Verlander — are reckoned to be in danger. The Herald files the Monday meeting under opening formalities, and keeps its register open.4

THE LAW COURTS: THE HOUSE ITSELF TAKES THE STAND IN BROOKLYN — FANDUEL'S MAN TESTIFIES THAT ACCOUNTS IN CLASE'S ORBIT WAGERED ON ORTIZ'S PITCHES TOO, ONE OF THEM COLLECTING TWELVE THOUSAND ON A SINGLE BALL THROWN WIDE

The federal trial of Emmanuel Clase and Luis Ortiz, whose opening testimony this paper's earlier dispatches from the Brooklyn courtroom set down, produced on Monday a witness from the counting-house side of the business. Joshua Mehta, director of legal and regulatory affairs for the house of FanDuel, testified that accounts registered to men linked to Clase during the trial placed heavy wagers on first pitches in two Cleveland games of June 2025 — on the 15th against Seattle and on the 27th against the Cardinals — and that Ortiz was the starting pitcher in both. The bettors risked thousands on the result of a specific pitch without knowing the batter, nor whether the starter would even still be on the hill.5

The particulars have a bookmaker's precision. Against Seattle, the house took a handful of wagers that the first pitch of the bottom of the third inning would be a ball or a hit batsman; several came from an account registered to Enoc Pena — the close associate of Clase's whom earlier testimony placed at the center of the scheme — and when Ortiz threw the pitch outside the strike zone, Pena's wagers collected approximately $12,000. Some of the same accounts bet big on Cleveland's first pitch of the third inning against the Cardinals twelve days later; that one, too, arrived wide. Mehta said at least five of the accounts were suspended in June 2025, the use of inside information being a violation of the house's terms — and the calendar duly records that Ortiz was placed on leave by the league on July 3, with Clase following roughly four weeks after.5

Earlier Monday the cooperating witness Jenner Olivo testified that he won bets on selected Clase pitches across the 2023, 2024 and 2025 seasons on information received from Pena; the government alleges the bettors took at least $400,000 on the result and speed of at least 18 Clase pitches. Both pitchers have pleaded not guilty to conspiracy charges touching wire fraud, sports bribery, honest services and money laundering. And the day closed on a stranger footnote: a FanDuel account registered to Clase himself, opened in May 2023, whose only recorded bets were on basketball — which, the record should note, no rule of the game forbids.5

THE EXCHANGE DESK: BOHM SITS DOWN WITH BOTH NEW YORKS, THE BIRDS DRAW A SHOPPING LIST WITH AROZARENA'S NAME AT ITS HEAD, AND THE WALKER PURCHASE SETS THE WIRE TO ASKING WHETHER MEGILL'S MILWAUKEE DAYS ARE NUMBERED

The corner infielder Alec Bohm has taken meetings with both New York establishments. The Athletic's Ken Rosenthal and Will Sammon report that the Yankees and the Metropolitans each sat with the former Philadelphia man at last week's meetings — and his season explains the double appeal. Bohm's season read a modest .698 in sum, but it concealed an .821 from August 4 onward, after the Quakers moved him across the diamond to first base; the Bronx men could platoon him at third with the left-handed McMahon, while the Mets, whose first basemen produced a .667 mark this past season, third-worst in the majors, might simply hand him the new position outright.6

In Baltimore the shopping list has grown long enough to publish. The Baltimore Banner's Andy Kostka reports the Birds interested in Randy Arozarena, the right-handed outfield bat their lefty-heavy order wants — though the man carries a qualifying offer, and signing him would cost a draft pick's toll to Seattle. Luis Robert Jr., whose $20 million option the club declined after his three-game, hamstring-shortened Baltimore tenure, remains a candidate to return at a friendlier wage; the club is operating with the intent of adding a left-handed starter, with Kris Bubic and Matthew Boyd of interest and a reunion with Trevor Rogers open — the same Rogers expected to decline his tender by this afternoon's deadline in search of a longer engagement. Calls have come in besides on the third baseman Jordan Westburg, and the Marte dialogue these columns recorded Sunday grinds on with no deal near.6

And in Milwaukee, Sunday's reclamation purchase is already casting its shadow. The wire asks plainly whether the acquisition of Ryan Walker — a man with ninth-inning experience and three years of control — makes Trevor Megill, entering his final year before free agency with 81 saves across the last three seasons, the more expendable; the Milwaukees have sold exactly this way before, sending Devin Williams to the Yankees ahead of his own walk year. The reader will note the wire's survey named Megill the club's likeliest man to go only yesterday in these columns; the drumbeat quickens. The left-hander A.J. Minter, meanwhile, has become one of the market's most pursued relievers, the insider Jon Paul Morosi counting the Jays, the Capital nine, the Phillies, the Rangers and the Royals among his suitors after a 2.56 season split between Queens and Minnesota; the Mets, who employed him last, have checked in as well.6

THE INK DESK: THE SPIDER-MAN OF THE CAPITAL GETS HIS FIGURES SET DOWN — YOUNG'S FOUR-YEAR ENGAGEMENT IS FINALIZED AT THREE-AND-TWENTY MILLIONS, AND IN THE DESERT, LAWLAR'S MENDED ELBOW IS EXPECTED BACK FOR THE SEASON'S OPENING

The quiet signature these columns recorded from Las Vegas on the twelfth now has its figures attached. The Nationals have finalized the four-year extension of their center fielder Jacob Young: $23 million guaranteed beginning in 2027, covering three of his arbitration years, with a club option at $8 million for 2031. It is the second extension of the young Toboni administration, following the four years and $47 million settled on the right-hander Cade Cavalli in September — brick by brick, the Capital nine are buying out the questions around their young core of Abrams, Wood, Crews and Lile.7

What the club has secured is the best wall-climber in the business. Young, 27, led all outfielders with 20 outs above average in 2024 and has followed with 14 and 11 in the two seasons since; the clubhouse calls him "Spider-Man," and the nickname earned its keep on August 23, when he covered 93 feet, scaled the wall at Miami, robbed Heriberto Hernández of a home run and threw back to the infield to finish a double play. The bat, long the asterisk on the profile, improved this past season to a .252 average with 10 home runs — doubling his career total at a stroke — a career-best 50 driven in, and 18 steals in 22 tries. A seventh-round selection paid like what he has become: a cornerstone of the game's third-highest-scoring offense.7

From the infirmary ward, one note out of the desert: Jordan Lawlar of the Desert nine underwent internal-brace surgery on his right elbow earlier this offseason, and the club expects the young man ready at or about the start of the regular season.8

THE ALMANAC: THE DAY OF ANSWERS IS AT HAND — SEVEN MEN MUST SPEAK FOR THREE-AND-TWENTY MILLIONS APIECE BY FOUR O'CLOCK THIS AFTERNOON, AND THE SILVER BATS ARE HANDED ROUND THIS EVENING

The day these columns have spent a week pointing toward has arrived. By 4 o'clock this afternoon, Eastern time, every man tendered the qualifying offer must answer: take the certain $23.15 million for 2027, or decline it and carry a draft pick's toll to any new employer. Eight were tendered; Jake Bauers answered early and in Boston's ink, as Saturday's lead recorded; seven answers remain outstanding. The roll deserves printing whole: Arozarena of Seattle, whose 148 OPS+ was the finest full-season figure of his career; Brandon Lowe of Pittsburgh, he of the 35 home runs and the remade glove; Seiya Suzuki of the Cubs, well above the league with the bat across his five American seasons; Rogers of the Birds, whose year away from one rough stretch read a 2.76; Morejon of the Mission nine, the first setup man ever so tendered; the catcher Jeffers of the Twins, quietly sixth among the position's regulars in OPS+ these past four seasons; and Bednar of the Bronx men, 35 saves in 39 chances. History counsels patience with predictions — since the system was instituted in 2012, just 18 men have ever accepted.9

The same evening brings the silver bats, whose finalists yesterday's columns arranged: Trout in pursuit of a tenth, a shelf only Piazza at ten and Bonds at twelve have reached.10 Answers and ornaments together, then — and the Herald will have the whole accounting, tenders and trophies alike, polished and arranged in tomorrow's columns.

A Tuesday that will answer more questions by nightfall than most Novembers answer in a week: seven tenders due by four o'clock, silver bats by evening, and a fresh Cooperstown ballot already circulating among the electors, as the lead column attests. The forward ledger was consulted before the first word, as the house requires, and shows what it showed: the camps' reporting dates await posting, so the count runs to the first rung bearing a date — the spring exhibition openers of Friday, the 19th of February, 94 mornings from this one, with Opening Night to follow on Wednesday, the 24th of March, 127 mornings off.1 The nearer columns of the almanac fill regardless: the collective agreement has 14 mornings left to live, the committee of sixteen reports from Cooperstown in 19, and the writers' envelope is opened in 63, on the 19th of January. The game plays nothing; the docket, meanwhile, has rarely been fuller. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

~ THE HERALD ~

entry.title: Hot Stove Edition — the Sixteenth of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? Not yet — 95 days until the first spring-training game.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 131 · Monday, the Sixteenth of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

No contests this day; the hot stove burns bright.

95 days until the first spring-training game (Friday, the 19th of February, 2027).

News Around the League

THE INK DESK: THE LINE FOR LEFT-HANDED RELIEF NEVER SHORTENS — SO THE BRONX DECLINES TO STAND IN IT, KEEPING HILL THE SUBMARINER FOR A YEAR AT TWO MILLIONS AND A QUARTER, THE FIRST BRICK LAID IN A BULLPEN ITS STEWARD CALLS THE WINTER'S MAIN PRIORITY

The Yankees' winter of relief work has begun at home. Tim Hill — the left-hander who delivers from down under, whose name stood in three clubs' notebooks when yesterday's columns surveyed the southpaw market, his admirers numbering the Dodgers, the Mets and his own employers — will stand in no line at all: man and club are agreed on a contract of one year and $2.25 million, with a club option at $2.5 million for 2028, the terms allowed by a source Sunday though the club had not yet confirmed them.2 It is the first move upon the bullpen whose rebuilding Brian Cashman declared, in the quote these columns carried Saturday, "It's our main priority, to be honest" — and the Herald observes that a paper which wrote only yesterday that the line for left-handed relief never shortens has been answered within the day: the simplest way to beat the queue is to own the merchandise already.

What the Pinstripes are keeping is the game's foremost dealer in groundballs. Hill, who turns 37 in January, pitched to a 4.60 earned-run average over 67 appearances and 58 and two-thirds innings this past season — an ordinary figure concealing an extraordinary trade, for his 68.9 percent ground-ball rate led every reliever in the Majors, he stranded 33 of the 35 runners he inherited, and the 5.7 percent of inherited men who came home against him was the stingiest figure in the game. Since New York claimed him in 2024, after a journeyman's road through Kansas City, San Diego and the South Side, he has given the club a 3.34 earned-run average across 172 appearances; the wage is modest, the angle is singular, and the fit is proven.2

The larger rebuilding remains. The Yankee bullpen's 3.13 earned-run average stood second-best in the Majors this past season, and much of it is now at liberty: David Bednar weighs the $23.15 million qualifying tender whose answer falls due tomorrow, with Paul Blackburn, Ryan Yarbrough, John Schreiber and Michael Fulmer free besides, and the club has rung the representatives of Adrian Morejon and of Jonathan Loáisiga — the same Loáisiga yesterday's columns reported nearing a verdict with five clubs bidding.2 The consolation of the market is its stock: the wire's survey of the winter's relievers calls the class at large a lean one but the relief shelf its deepest, with Morejon at the head of it — so the shoppers, in the Bronx and everywhere else, will find the store open all winter.3

THE CHAMPIONS' LEDGER: THE WORLD'S CHAMPIONS SEND TWO ARMS WEST FOR ONE THAT LOST ITS WAY — WALKER, ONCE AMONG THE LEAGUE'S BEST FIREMEN AND LATELY OF THE GIANTS' CELLAR, IS BOOKED INTO THE SAME ESTABLISHMENT THAT MADE MEGILL, WHILE THE WIRE NAMES MEGILL HIMSELF THE WINTER'S LIKELIEST MAN TO GO

Milwaukee has taken in another reclamation. By Sunday's business the champions acquired the right-hander Ryan Walker from the Giants for two minor-league arms — Blake Holub, 28, who pitched to a 2.10 earned-run average with five saves across 50 games at Nashville, and Gavin Perry, 23, an 11th-round selection of the summer's draft who has yet to throw a professional pitch — and the manager made no secret of the method. Pat Murphy likens his pitching laboratory to the "H&H Car Wash," the initials belonging to the coaches Chris Hook and Jim Henderson, who take in arms that have lost their shine and return them gleaming; the establishment's famous customer is Trevor Megill, fetched from obscurity in a minor trade of 2023 after indifferent service with the Cubs and the Twins, and lately the man who recorded the final six outs of the World's Series.4

Walker arrives wanting exactly that treatment. In 2024 he was among the best relief pitchers alive — a 1.91 earned-run average over 76 appearances, ten wins to lead all National League relievers, ten saves, a 0.85 walks-and-hits figure — and in 2026 he was among the most lost, a 7.16 earned-run average in 33 appearances before San Francisco sent him down in May to shuttle between the Bay and the minors. He turns 31 ten mornings hence, on November 26, carries three years of club control, and cost two arms the champions could spare: a wager on the car wash, at the car wash's usual price.4 The bullpen book he joins holds Megill in his final year of arbitration alongside Abner Uribe, Aaron Ashby, DL Hall and Chad Patrick, with Antonio Senzatela and JoJo Romero at liberty — and the reader should mark that the wire's man, surveying trade candidates for all thirty clubs this morning, names Megill himself the champion likeliest to be moved, three mornings after the front office serenaded him in these columns from a Metallica concert at the Sphere.5 The telephone in Milwaukee, as this paper has observed of the catcher Contreras, does not distinguish between the men it rings for.

The rotation behind them poses the winter's quieter question: which Kyle Harrison reports to the spring. Through 11 starts the young left-hander owned a 1.57 earned-run average with 73 strikeouts in 57 and a third innings — second in the game in strikeouts per nine — before a forearm complaint and an August return that found the fastball dimmed; from August onward he pitched to a 7.31 figure over 32 innings and finished the season in the bullpen, unused through October. The ailment was reckoned mild, the underlying numbers kinder than the surface ones, and the house arithmetic is plain: the April version makes a front three with Misiorowski and Logan Henderson, while Woodruff and May sit among the free agents.6

THE PINSTRIPE VACANCY: CHISHOLM GOES TO MARKET UNTENDERED AND SECOND BASE STANDS OPEN IN THE BRONX — THE WIRE NOMINATES LOWE OF THE SMOKY CITY, WHOSE FIVE-AND-THIRTY HOME RUNS WERE DRAWN, NEARLY EVERY ONE, TOWARD A PORCH LIKE THE ONE AT THE STADIUM

The same Bronx front office keeping its left-hander has a vacancy up the middle. Jazz Chisholm Jr. has gone to the open market after two seasons and more in pinstripes, and the club declined to attach a qualifying offer to him — a quiet verdict of its own, for the tender it did extend went to the closer Bednar. Chisholm's season explains the hesitation: 19 home runs with a .399 slugging mark, the underlying measurements grading his contact at a .366 expected slug, down in the 24th percentile of the league, though his glovework at second — 15 outs above average, the best of his career — will be missed by a defense that can ill spare it. The internal answers are familiar: Anthony Volpe, who moved to second when young George Lombard Jr. took shortstop, with the utility men José Caballero and Luis García Jr. behind him.7

The wire's suggestion is Brandon Lowe, the left-handed second baseman who struck 35 home runs with an .824 on-base-plus-slugging for Pittsburgh this past season — a Ray for seven and a half years before the Smoky City nine acquired him in mid-2025.8 The case is a matter of architecture. Of his 35 home runs, 32 went to right field, pulled in the air at a career-high rate — and he compiled them in the yard the statisticians rank 27th of 30 for the long ball, while Yankee Stadium, with its short right porch, ranks among the friendliest; by Statcast's reckoning the same batted balls at the Stadium would have numbered 39. Nor is the glove the liability it was: from ten runs below average in 2025 he swung to twelve above in 2026, third-best at the position and a finalist for the National League's Gold Glove, tied for the largest year-over-year turnaround the measurers have recorded. For a lineup that hit 223 home runs, second-most in the game, yet batted ten percent below league average while Judge convalesced from the first of June to the seventh of September — only the Angels fared worse in that stretch — the appeal writes itself. The club enters its 18th year without a championship, tied for the longest such passage since Ruth came over in 1919; the winter's shopping list, bullpen first and second base close behind, is drawn up accordingly.7

THE EXCHANGE DESK: ONE NAME PINNED TO EVERY CLUBHOUSE DOOR — THE WIRE'S MAN NOMINATES A TRADE CANDIDATE FOR ALL THIRTY CLUBS, AND THE HERALD FINDS HALF ITS WINTER'S STORYLINES ALREADY ON THE LIST

The wire's senior correspondent has performed the winter's great parlor exercise — one plausible trade candidate named for every club in the land — and the Herald, reading down the list, keeps meeting its own back pages.5 Jarren Duran stands for Boston, the outfielder an evaluator called "clearly available" in Saturday's columns, his outfield crowded further by the Bauers purchase. Shane McClanahan stands for the Tampa men, confirming the sorting these pages recorded Saturday of the pennant-winners' rotation into the kept and the biddable. Ketel Marte stands for the Snakes — the twice-silvered second baseman whose dialogue with Baltimore filled yesterday's columns, his ten-and-five veto noted in the same breath — and for the Baltimores themselves the nominee is Jackson Holliday, the young infielder whose September wrist surgery helped open the very vacancy Marte would fill: the buyer's own candidate, in other words, is the price the seller may ask. George Kirby stands for the mariners of the Sound, one of the two names these columns reckoned likeliest to be had when Dipoto allowed on Friday that his rotation was eight deep and his lineup listing.5

The fresher entries concern the coasts. For the Dodgers the nominee is Teoscar Hernández, whose departure would clear a garden spot for the prospect Josue De Paula; for the Yankees it is Jasson Domínguez, the once-celebrated young outfielder still without a settled station, squeezed now by the arrival of Spencer Jones. Add the champions' Megill, treated in the column above, and the exercise reads less like speculation than like a timetable: the names the winter has been circling, now written down in one place.5

THE ALMANAC: THE SEVENTEENTH ARRIVES ON THE MORROW BEARING ANSWERS AND SILVERWARE TOGETHER — QUALIFYING VERDICTS FALL DUE AT LAST, AND THE SILVER BATS ARE HANDED ROUND WITH TROUT IN PURSUIT OF A TENTH, COMPANY ONLY PIAZZA AND BONDS HAVE KEPT

The appointment this paper's calendar has carried for a week arrives tomorrow, and it is a double one. The qualifying offers meet their deadline: Bednar of the Yankees and Morejon of the Padres are among the men still dragging the $23.15 million tender behind them, and by evening each must take the certain money or the open market — the reader will recall that Bauers answered his tender early, in Boston's ink, and that the compensation machinery has already begun to grind in Milwaukee.2

The same evening brings the silver bats. The Silver Slugger awards, whose finalists were posted on the fifth of the month, are to be revealed tomorrow, and the ornament of the slate is Mike Trout: the old master seeks his tenth silver bat, a shelf only Mike Piazza, with ten, and Barry Bonds, with twelve, have ever reached, and his case is honest — an .803 on-base-plus-slugging across 142 games, his best figure in ten years. Elsewhere among the finalists stand the newly laureled Alvarez, who led the game in each leg of the batting line; Alonso of the Baltimores and his league-best 43 home runs; and Bauers again, nominated at first base and in the utility class alike — while the team prize for the best offense in each league pits the Astros, Tampa men, Twins and White Sox in the American against the champions, the Cubs, the Boys in Blue and the Nationals in the National.9 The Herald will have the verdicts in Wednesday's columns, polished and arranged.

A Monday on which the winter kept its shops open through the weekend: a left-hander retained in the Bronx, a reclamation project carted into Milwaukee, and the morrow's docket already posted, as the almanac column attests — qualifying answers and silver bats together on the seventeenth. The forward ledger was ruled open before a word was written, per the house custom, and stands unchanged: the camps' reporting dates are still to be posted, so the paper counts to the first rung bearing a date — the spring exhibition openers of Friday, the 19th of February, 95 mornings from this one — with Opening Night to follow on Wednesday, the 24th of March, 128 mornings off.1 Nearer at hand, the collective agreement has 15 mornings left to live, and Cooperstown's sixteen electors report their verdict on December 6, 20 mornings from this one. The game plays nothing and decides everything, which is November's whole constitution. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: Hot Stove Edition — the Fifteenth of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? Not yet — 96 days until the first spring-training game.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 130 · Sunday, the Fifteenth of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

No contests this day; the hot stove burns bright.

96 days until the first spring-training game (Friday, the 19th of February, 2027).

News Around the League

THE PROSPECT FIELDS: PEORIA TAKES THE DESERT'S LAST PRIZE — THE JAVELINAS BREAK SURPRISE 8-3 FOR AN EIGHTH FALL LEAGUE CROWN, THE MOST IN THE CIRCUIT'S BOOKS AND THEIR FIRST SINCE 2018, BEHIND FIVE SCORELESS INNINGS FROM HOLMAN OF THE QUEEN CITY CHAIN

The desert kept its appointment. The Fall League championship that Saturday's columns commended to every restless scorecard hand was decided at the Peoria Sports Complex on Saturday night, and it was the home club's evening throughout: the Peoria Javelinas 8, the Surprise Saguaros 3, and the title — an eighth for Peoria, the most any club has gathered in the circuit's history and its first since 2018 — was denied to the defending champions, finalists now seven autumns running. The occasion extended one of the minor calendar's quieter marvels besides: one of these two clubs has appeared in the title game in each of the last 17 seasons, the last final without either being played in 2008. Carter Graham of Cincinnati's chain supplied the victors' epigraph, shouting to anyone in earshot, "Best team in the nation, baby!"2

Luke Holman, whom Saturday's columns sent to the hill trailing a 0.69 earned-run average, pitched precisely to the billing: five scoreless innings, six strikeouts, 16 swings-and-misses drawn across three offerings — a fastball at 92 to 94 mph, a splitter, a curve — and the game's honors as its best player. The evening's loudest contact belonged to his systemmate Yerlin Confidan, the Fall Stars Game's Most Valuable man, who ripped a single at 116.7 mph and a double at 110.3 in a 3-for-4 night, while Graham added two singles and a walk. Justin DeCriscio of the San Diego chain lined an RBI double, Brandon Eike of the Seattle chain another; Ike Irish, the young Baltimore outfielder whose sacrifice fly had won the semifinal, went hitless yet scored twice, drove in a run and stole a bag; Kannon Kemp threw the 13 hardest pitches of the night across two scoreless innings of relief; and Francis Peña ran his heater to 97.5 mph in the ninth to lock the trophy away.2

The champions' ledger reads like a period of its own: 219 runs scored, the most of any club across the six-week term, and 112 stolen bases in 28 games — 16 clear of the next-nearest club, the circuit having experimented this autumn with a single disengagement per plate appearance. The whole enterprise answered to Danny Worth, a man of parts of six big-league seasons who had never managed at any level before this fall, and who, dripping with the remains of the water cooler, allowed that he might simply retire on top: "We're gonna be watching all these guys on TV for a long time." And the autumn's individual laurel went where these columns said it belonged — Welbyn Francisca of the Lake Erie chain, whose .427 average led the league, was named winner of the Joe Black Award as its Most Valuable player, a consolation carried home in Surprise's otherwise empty luggage.2

THE EXCHANGE DESK: THE FRIARS, SHORT SEVEN STARTERS, GO COURTING EVERY ARM AT LIBERTY — A SITTING WITH SKUBAL IS BOOKED, OLD FRIENDS KING AND PIVETTA ARE EYED FOR REUNION, AND THE DODGERS JOIN A FIVE-CLUB QUEUE FOR LOÁISIGA

San Diego's winter brief is written in a single line of its general manager's: "you can never have too much" starting pitching — and A.J. Preller, who is losing seven starting pitchers to free agency at a stroke, is conducting himself accordingly. The Friars stand among the most active clubs in the starters' market and are leaving no door unknocked: a meeting is booked with Tarik Skubal himself, adding San Diego's name formally to the suitors' register these columns have kept all week; reunions are eyed with Michael King and Nick Pivetta, former men of the Mission both; and the club has expressed interest in Freddy Peralta — the right-hander who rediscovered his best self after the midseason trade to Tampa Bay and carried the honors of the league championship series in October — as well as Nick Martinez, whose career-best year read 31 starts, a first All-Star nod and the Game 1 assignment of the World Series, and who pitched to a 3.45 earned-run average in San Diego colors in 2022 and 2023. The register runs on: Matthew Boyd, Shota Imanaga and Dustin May — the last of whom yesterday's columns called the most democratically courted arm of the winter after Skubal — have all had their doors knocked as well.3

The relief market, meanwhile, nears its first verdict. Jonathan Loáisiga is reported "getting closer" to his next contract, with five clubs in the bidding — the Dodgers, Phillies, Mets, Yankees and Jays — for a right arm that rebounded from two injury-ruined seasons to a 2.42 earned-run average over 67 appearances in Arizona's employ. The Dodgers are also named among the pursuers of Tim Hill, the submarining left-hander lately of the Bronx, whose admirers include the Mets and his former Yankee employers besides — for in this winter's market, as in every winter's, the line for left-handed relief never shortens.3

THE SONORAN QUESTION, A SECOND WINTER RUNNING: THE BIRDS COME CALLING FOR MARTE — BALTIMORE AND ARIZONA ARE IN DIALOGUE ON THE TWICE-SILVERED SECOND BASEMAN, NO DEAL NEAR, AND THE MAN HIMSELF HOLDS THE VETO

The Marte question, which these columns found reopened at Las Vegas on Thursday, has produced its first named suitor. The Orioles have dialogued with the Diamondbacks regarding Ketel Marte — so a source allowed on Saturday evening — though no deal was imminent and neither club would confirm the discussions; the Jays, shopping for hitters generally, are reported among the interested as well. Arizona's steward Mike Hazen has supplied the winter's framing himself: "I just think I need to be open to making adjustments to what the roster looks like."43

The fit at Baltimore is at once obvious and awkward. Obvious, because the Birds drew a collective .628 on-base-plus-slugging from second base this past season, the fourth-worst figure in the majors, while Jackson Holliday, 22, long cast as the second baseman of the future, fought injuries culminating in September wrist surgery. Awkward, because the infield house is already crowded — so crowded that Mike Elias allows the club has spoken with some infielders about taking outfield work this spring. Yet Baltimore has shown exactly this appetite before: a year ago it wanted no first baseman and signed Pete Alonso to five years and $155 million anyway, a purchase that has aged handsomely.4

As for the man, the ledger states the case plainly. Marte is 33, a three-time All-Star and twice a Silver Slugger, a .277 hitter across 1,371 games with 193 home runs and an .815 on-base-plus-slugging; this past season he batted .249 with 22 home runs and a .748 mark in 141 games, around a brief August stay on the restricted list after failing to appear for a game at Fenway Park — an absence of some two weeks, closed with an apology to his manager and his teammates and a quiet, blameless remainder of the season. Four guaranteed years remain on his $116.5 million extension, with a player option for 2031 behind them, and his ten years of service — the last five in one uniform — give him the veto over any destination proposed. The desert may open the question; only Marte can close it.4

THE TRADE WINDS BLOW THROUGH SHORTSTOP COUNTRY — CALLERS RING THE WHITE ELEPHANTS ON WILSON, THE LONE STAR NINE LISTEN ON SEAGER, AND THE FISH FIELD OFFERS ON THREE YOUNG REGULARS AT ONCE

The winter's trade talk has found the game's middle infield. Bob Nightengale of USA TODAY reports that clubs have called the Athletics to inquire after Jacob Wilson — a name that would have seemed untouchable a year ago, when the shortstop batted .311 as a rookie, became the first rookie shortstop ever elected by the fans to start an All-Star Game for the American League, and finished second in the Rookie of the Year balloting to his own teammate Nick Kurtz. The Elephants extended him for seven years and $70 million before the 2026 season, control running through at least 2032; the season that followed is the reason the callers think it worth dialing — a .266 average over just 80 games, three separate trips to the injured list, and a nagging left shoulder that ended his year in mid-August. He turns 25 in March. Elsewhere in the shortstop country, the Lone Star nine are reportedly listening on Corey Seager, while Washington's CJ Abrams is held unlikely to move.3

And in Miami, Barry Jackson of the Miami Herald reports the Fish fielding offers on three young regulars at once: the middle infielders Otto Lopez and Xavier Edwards — for whom the club "would want a ton to even consider moving" either — and the first baseman and outfielder Kyle Stowers. The asking prices have their reasons. Lopez, 28, was a first-time All-Star who led the majors with 191 hits, stole 34 bases and saved 14 outs above average at shortstop; Edwards, 27, batted .280 with a .360 on-base mark and 21 steals, worth three wins above replacement in each of the past two seasons; Stowers, 28, struck 21 home runs with a .790 on-base-plus-slugging through hamstring strains in each leg, a year after 25 and .912. All three are under club control through 2029 — which is precisely why the offers keep arriving, and precisely why Miami need accept none of them.3

THE COOPERSTOWN DESK: EIGHT NAMES GO BEFORE THE SIXTEEN — BOCHY OF THE FOUR TITLES AND MADDON OF THE BROKEN CURSE HEAD THE CONTEMPORARY ERA BALLOT, WITH BAKER, PINIELLA, ALDERSON, SABEAN, TURNER AND WHITE BESIDE THEM, THE VERDICT DUE THE SIXTH OF DECEMBER

The village on Otsego Lake has posted its winter docket. The Contemporary Baseball Era ballot — the committee's turn, this cycle, to weigh managers, executives and umpires — carries eight names: Sandy Alderson, Dusty Baker, Bruce Bochy, Joe Maddon, Lou Piniella, Brian Sabean, Ted Turner and Bill White. A 16-member panel of Hall of Fame players, executives, writers and historians will sit in judgment, twelve votes of the sixteen being required for election, and the results for the Class of 2027 are to be announced on December 6 — 21 mornings from this one.56

Two managers head the bill. Bochy's credentials scarcely require the committee's reading glasses: 2,252 wins, sixth on the all-time roll, with the five men above him — Mack, La Russa, McGraw, Cox and Torre — already enshrined; four World Series titles, making him the sixth manager to win so many and the first to do it for two clubs, the fourth ring fetched from retirement in his first Texas summer. "It's unthinkable for something like this to happen," says the man, 71, with a catcher's modesty. Maddon's case is the romantic's: 1,382 wins across parts of 19 seasons in Tampa Bay, Chicago and Anaheim — one of 35 managers to reach 1,300, and one of only 16 of those to win at a .532 clip or better — three Manager of the Year awards, two pennants, and the 2016 championship that ended the North Siders' 108-year wait, delivered by a man who governed with mantras ("9=8," "Try Not to Suck") and wore No. 70 on his back. His partisans have already minted the campaign slogan: Respect 70.5

The Herald notes, for the completeness of the record, that the remaining six names span the game's whole administration — Baker and Piniella from the dugout, Alderson and Sabean from the front office, Turner from the owner's box and White from the league presidency — and that a committee's arithmetic is harder than a season's. Eight worthies, sixteen electors, and three weeks to the envelope.5

A Sunday of consequence for the almanac: with the desert's trophy handed over, as the lead column records, the last diamond in the land occupied by big-league organizations has gone dark,2 and the American game is now, until the camps open, a matter of ledgers, telephones and ballots. The forward ledger was ruled open before a word was written, per the house custom, and stands unchanged: the camps' reporting dates are still to be posted, so the paper counts to the first rung bearing a date — the spring exhibition openers of Friday, the 19th of February, 96 mornings from this one — with Opening Night to follow on Wednesday, the 24th of March, 129 mornings off.1 The nearer appointments crowd the book regardless: Tuesday the 17th brings the qualifying answers and the silver bats together, as this paper's calendar has long carried; the collective agreement has 16 mornings left to live; and Cooperstown's sixteen electors report their verdict on December 6. The game has stopped playing, but it has by no means stopped keeping score. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

~ THE HERALD ~

entry.title: Hot Stove Edition — the Fourteenth of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? Not yet — 97 days until the first spring-training game.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 129 · Saturday, the Fourteenth of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

No contests this day; the hot stove burns bright.

97 days until the first spring-training game (Friday, the 19th of February, 2027).

News Around the League

THE INK DESK: THE ANSWER ARRIVES FOUR DAYS EARLY — BAUERS, HERO OF THE LATE OCTOBER, TAKES EIGHT-AND-FIFTY MILLIONS OVER FOUR YEARS FROM THE CRIMSON HOSE, AND THE CHAMPIONS, WHO KNOW THIS RITUAL BY HEART, STAND TO POCKET A PREMIUM PICK FOR THEIR TROUBLE

The answer was not due until Tuesday. The qualifying offer that Milwaukee tendered its first baseman carried a deadline of the 17th — an appointment this paper's ledger has kept all week — and Jake Bauers answered it four days early, in another club's ink. The Red Sox and the hero of the late October have agreed on a contract of four years and $58 million, pending a physical, the figures confirmed to MLB.com's Mark Feinsand after ESPN's Jeff Passan first carried the report: the largest signature of the young offseason, and the first of the winter's dominoes to fall with an audible report.23 The purchase is Boston doctrine made flesh. Craig Breslow, the president of baseball operations, had lately observed that a club without obvious holes must be "open-minded, flexible and opportunistic" in its improving, and an attack that finished 26th in home runs and 20th in slugging has now bought itself the most patient bat on the open market.2

What the Fenway men are buying is a career year with the receipts to argue it no accident. Bauers, 30, batted .266 with a .389 on-base mark and a .484 slug across 578 plate appearances, struck a team-high 26 home runs and drove in 86; he walked at a 16.3 percent rate that stood in the 98th percentile of the league, and by the Statcast ledger he hit the ball harder than ever in his life — an average exit speed of 92.1 mph, a hard-hit rate of 51.9 percent, a barrel rate of 14 percent, every one of them above the 90th percentile — though the whiffs remain plentiful, his 27 percent strikeout rate being the price of the patience.2 October wants no retelling in these columns, but shall have a little anyway: the 12-pitch walk that set up the second game's victory in the league championship set, the go-ahead clout off Blake Snell at the end of an 11-pitch audience in the third, the series' Most Valuable honor as the Suds men swept the two-time defending titleholders of Los Angeles — and a quiet Fall Classic that mattered not at all, his club winning it in five. Nor should the romance beneath the figures go unrecorded: after the 2024 season, when he batted .199, Bauers was minded to give the game up entirely, until his wife, Lauren, revealed she was expecting, and the man reconsidered. Two years from that crossroads he is a champion with $58 million in promised wages.2 The fit at Boston is a winter's puzzle happily deferred — Willson Contreras keeps first base, the designated place is shared with Masataka Yoshida in the final year of his engagement — but the Monster's wall stands 310 feet from the plate, and Bauers' habit of taking his singles and doubles the other way will find it a friendly neighbor.2

And in Milwaukee, the ritual plays out precisely as the house has rehearsed it. Because the Cream City men extended their qualifying offer and the man signed elsewhere for more than $50 million, they stand to receive a compensation pick between the end of the first round and the start of Competitive Balance Round A in next summer's draft — the same toll collected when Willy Adames took the Giants' $182 million two winters ago, a toll that became the 32nd pick and the prep shortstop Brady Ebel, today the fourth-ranked prospect in their system.4 The succession at first base is already sketched: Andrew Vaughn, the right-handed half of the late platoon, enters his final year of arbitration, and the minors offer Blake Burke, 23, a left-handed hitter who struck 34 home runs between Biloxi and Nashville this past season.4 The method — the contract-year man exchanged for tomorrow, which yesterday's columns rehearsed in the catcher's context — has thus claimed its newest entry, and the question those columns weighed concerning William Contreras acquires a sharper edge this morning: Milwaukee has now lost the first baseman who handed its manager the final-out ball, and the telephone about the catcher has not stopped ringing.

THE EXCHANGE DESK: THE WRIGLEY MEN GO SHOPPING FOR A ROTATION ENTIRE AND KNOCK ON FIVE DOORS AT ONCE, BOSTON'S NEW PURCHASE CROWDS ITS OWN HOUSE, THE GULF COAST CLUB KEEPS ITS ACE AND LEAVES TWO OTHERS ON THE SHELF IN VIEW, AND MORE THAN HALF THE LEAGUE COMES CALLING FOR ONE LEFT ARM

The Cubs' predicament, which these columns set out yesterday — a unanimous laureate in center field and not one incumbent starting pitcher — now has a shopping list attached. To the five free agents of the late rotation add the swingman Colin Rea, also at liberty, and Jameson Taillon, moved along in August: seven arms that made 121 starts for Chicago this past season, all gone, with Javier Assad the lone returning starter coming off a healthy year.5 The register of targets runs wide: Michael King, a pairing the MLB Network's man calls long forecasted; Kaima Taira, the Japanese right-hander who led his league with a 1.36 earned-run average over 146 innings, in whom Chicago's interest is reported strong; Freddy Peralta, whom Craig Counsell managed for years in Milwaukee and whom the Athletic's correspondent calls an obvious fit; Trevor Rogers; and Dustin May. The club is also said to want Clay Holmes and David Peterson back from its own departed shelf.5

May, as it happens, is the winter's most democratically courted arm — the pitcher drawing the most interest at the meetings after Skubal himself, with the Cubs, White Sox, Padres, Astros and Marlins all in the circle. His 4.70 earned-run average across 145 and two-thirds innings for St. Louis and Milwaukee is no ornament, but the velocity has climbed back toward its early-career marks, his strikeout-minus-walk figure was a five-year best, and at 29 he is among the youngest starters at liberty.5 At Boston, meanwhile, the morning's lead item casts its shadow sideways: with Bauers installed and Contreras at first, the house is crowded, and the trade talk now turns on Jarren Duran — "clearly available," one National League evaluator says of the oft-rumored outfielder, though his cratered season and climbing wage complicate the return — and on the squeezed first baseman Triston Casas, whose accustomed stations are now doubly occupied.5 And on the Gulf Coast, the pennant-winners have sorted their rotation into the kept and the biddable: Erik Neander professes "every intention" of holding his ace Drew Rasmussen, whose $20 million option — the largest single-season wage in the franchise's books — was exercised last month, while the trade reports a deal involving Shane McClanahan or Ryan Pepiot a live possibility, both men lately acquainted with the surgeon and each a year or two from the open market.5

The relief market, where the only actual ink of the meetings was spilled — Phillips, Pagán and Weiss, all chronicled in these columns this week — still holds its marquee names: David Bednar and Adrian Morejon, each dragging a qualifying offer behind him, with Raisel Iglesias and Kenley Jansen at liberty besides. In the Bronx the matter is declared urgent. "It's our main priority, to be honest," Brian Cashman says of his bullpen, two of whose three late-innings keepers — Bednar, tendered at $23.15 million, and Paul Blackburn — are free agents: "I am casting a wide net. We are asking around, and we need to find some stuff so we can feel good and sleep at night."6 The Yankees would have Morejon should Bednar walk, and would keep their left-hander Tim Hill — the same Hill the Mets are sniffing at, that club being linked to nearly every southpaw at liberty: Hill, Brooks Raley, A.J. Minter and Alex Vesia, the last of whom is reported to interest more than half the clubs in the league. One left arm, and a queue at the door sixteen clubs long at the least: the winter's arithmetic in miniature.5

THE DUGOUT DESK: AUSMUS TAKES THE HOUSTON CHAIR WITH BAGWELL AND BIGGIO IN THE FRONT ROW — A FOUR-HOUR LUNCH AT SAN DIEGO SEALED THE MATCH, AND THE NEW MAN DECLINES ALL TALK OF GLORY DAYS

The homecoming this paper recorded on Thursday was made ceremonial on Friday. Brad Ausmus was introduced as manager of the Astros at Daikin Park, with Jeff Bagwell and Craig Biggio, his old teammates, seated in the front row — and the story behind the hiring, told at last, turns out to have begun with a disappointment. Ausmus left the park on October 29 after interviewing for the general manager's position and told his wife, Liz, he did not expect to get it; he was right, Randy Flores being hired a day later. But Flores telephoned within days, offered to travel to San Diego, and the two men clicked over a four-hour lunch — Flores having first done his diligence through, among others, Aaron Boone, his college teammate and lately Ausmus's employer in the Yankee coaching rooms.7

The introduction had its vaudeville — Flores, a pitcher in his playing days, asked from the dais whether Ausmus had owned him at the plate, and got back "I was 0-for-1 with a walk, and that's the truth" — but the new manager kept the sentiment on a short leash. "Looking back on my career, if I picture myself, it's wearing an Astros uniform," he said. "That being said, I'm not here to talk about the glory days. I'm here to talk about the Astros today, and the Astros going into 2027, which is now my main focus, and certainly the goal is to win the World Series." The work is considerable: a coaching staff to assemble, a bench coach first among the vacancies, and a roster that, for all the pleasure of writing the newly laureled Alvarez into the middle of its order, was swept from October's opening round and wants improving in several departments. Berkman and Oswalt have already rung with congratulations; the Herald suspects the congratulatory period will be brief.7

THE FAR PACIFIC DESK: THE EASTBOUND TRAFFIC THICKENS — KOO, MOST VALUABLE OF THE KOREAN SERIES, ENGAGES AN AGENT TO TRY THE AMERICAN MARKET AT FOUR-AND-THIRTY

The procession across the Pacific, which brought Teruaki Sato's name to these columns on Tuesday and Kaima Taira's to the exchange desk above, now adds a Korean chapter. Ja-Wook Koo, the 33-year-old corner outfielder of the Samsung Lions — he turns 34 in February — has engaged Jaron Long of the Mako Corporation to explore a move to the Majors.8 The credentials are a batting champion's: a .371 average this past season, the best in his league, with a .458 on-base mark, 15 home runs and 102 driven in across 114 games, his 1.039 OPS standing third among the circuit's qualified hitters; and when the Lions reached the Korean Series he batted .500 over the five-game set and was named its Most Valuable man. A left-handed hitter twelve seasons in the same uniform, he brings a career line of .322, which is the sort of number that travels well in any language. Where the younger Sato commands projections running toward nine figures, Koo's age makes him the value proposition of the eastbound register — and the Herald, which has watched this winter's market grow more international by the morning, adds his name to the watch list with pleasure.8

THE PROSPECT FIELDS: THE DESERT CROWNS ITS CHAMPION THIS EVENING — SURPRISE, SEVEN TIMES RUNNING A FINALIST, MEETS PEORIA FOR THE FALL LEAGUE TITLE BEHIND A SEMIFINAL IN WHICH ONE MAN DROVE HOME SEVEN

The prospect calendar of 2026 closes this very evening. The Arizona Fall League, finishing school of the rising class, stages its championship game tonight at the Peoria Sports Complex, 8 o'clock Eastern on the MLB Network: the Surprise Saguaros, in the final for a seventh consecutive autumn, against the Peoria Javelinas, whom they beat for last year's title — the two clubs having posted the circuit's two best records besides.9 The semifinals supplied their own theater. Cole Mathis, a first baseman in the Mets' chain, drove in seven runs — a Fall League playoff record — in Surprise's 10-4 dispatch of Glendale, while Peoria edged Salt River 6-5 on a decisive sacrifice fly from Ike Irish, the Orioles' young outfielder.9

The pitching assignment alone recommends the broadcast: Peoria sends Luke Holman of Cincinnati's system, who returned from elbow surgery to lead the league in earned-run average at 0.69 and hold the desert's hitters to a .114 average, against Justin Lamkin of the Kansas City chain. And whatever this evening decides, the autumn's breakout belongs already to Welbyn Francisca of Cleveland's system, who led the circuit in hitting at .427, in slugging, in OPS, in hits, in total bases and in runs driven in — a $1.375 million signing out of the Dominican Republic making a loud case for larger stages. The Herald commends the fixture to any reader whose scorecard hand has grown restless these sixteen gameless mornings.9

A Saturday on which the winter found its voice. The silver season adjourned Thursday night; by Friday afternoon the market had produced its first great signature, as the lead column attests, and the desk observes that the sport allowed itself scarcely a night's repose between the last trophy and the first fortune. The forward ledger was ruled open before a word was written, per the house custom, and it stands as it stood: the camps' reporting dates are still to be posted, so the paper counts to the first rung with a date on it — the spring exhibition slate of Friday, the 19th of February, 97 mornings from this one, with Opening Night to follow 130 mornings off, on Wednesday, the 24th of March.1 Nearer at hand, the desert plays its Fall League championship this very evening, as the prospect column records, and the 17th keeps its appointment three mornings hence — qualifying answers and silver bats together — though one answer, as the reader now knows, has already come back early and addressed to Boston. The collective agreement has 17 mornings left to live, and the week's dealings suggest the clubs intend to spend them busily. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: Hot Stove Edition — the Thirteenth of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? Not yet — 98 days until the first spring-training game.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 128 · Friday, the Thirteenth of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

No contests this day; the hot stove burns bright.

98 days until the first spring-training game (Friday, the 19th of February, 2027).

News Around the League

THE LAURELS DESK: THE LAST ENVELOPES OF THE SILVER SEASON — ALVAREZ OF HOUSTON AND CROW-ARMSTRONG OF THE NORTH SIDE ARE NAMED MOST VALUABLE ON ALL THIRTY BALLOTS APIECE, AND FOR THE FIRST TIME IN ALL THE YEARS SINCE THE PITCHERS' PRIZE WAS STRUCK, EVERY ONE OF THE SEASON'S FOUR GREAT HONORS IS UNANIMOUS

One of them does his damage standing nearly still, the heaviest bat in the American League attached to a man who took the field just 25 times; the other plays center field like a sentry posted over the whole garden, and runs, and throws, and hits for power besides. Asked to choose between impact in its purest form and impact in all its forms, the writers declined to vote against either: the Baseball Writers' Association of America read its Most Valuable verdicts Thursday night, and Yordan Alvarez of the Astros and Pete Crow-Armstrong of the Cubs were named first on every ballot cast in their leagues — the fourteenth unanimous choice in the American League's history and the eleventh in the National's, and only the third November, after 2023 and 2024, in which both Most Valuable prizes went without dissent.23 Set Wednesday's sweep by Misiorowski and Schlittler beside it and the week closes on a thing never before entered in the books: since the pitchers' prize was struck in 1956, no season had ever seen both Most Valuable awards and both Cy Youngs voted unanimously together.5 The reader will recall that Wednesday's theater at Las Vegas handed its Aaron awards to precisely these two men, and that yesterday's columns called them the favorites by the wire's reckoning; the ballot has now ratified what the hint already whispered.4

Alvarez's season was a masterclass in the oldest arts. He led all the Majors in each of the three figures a batting line is built from — a .316 average, a .432 on-base mark, a .607 slug — just the fourth man this century to do it, after Barry Bonds in 2002, Miguel Cabrera in 2013 and Aaron Judge only last year, and he was walked intentionally 33 times, a Houston record and the second-most in American League history behind Judge's 36 of 2025.4 The one prize that escaped him was the Triple Crown, which came apart in September: his 42 home runs and 106 driven in each finished second to Pete Alonso of the Orioles, one shy and seven shy respectively — though he is only the third man since 1970 to take the American League batting title while hitting 40 home runs, after Cabrera and Judge. He is the second man whose trade is chiefly designated hitting ever to win the award, following the door Shohei Ohtani broke down; the fourth Cuban-born Most Valuable, after José Abreu, Jose Canseco and Zoilo Versalles; and the third Astro so honored, after Jeff Bagwell in 1994 and Jose Altuve in 2017 — with only Bagwell, like him, unanimous.45 The trophy completes a week in which he also carried off the Aaron award, the Edgar Martínez prize and the league's Comeback honor. "I just wanted a chance," he said through an interpreter, of the boy in Cuba who dreamed smaller than this. "I wanted a chance to play professional baseball years ago. Winning the MVP, winning the World Series, none of this was in my mind. So to be here now … look at me now."4

Crow-Armstrong's case was the whole toolbox, and it was built from a ruin. A third of the way through the schedule the young Cub carried a .673 OPS — the lowest figure, by the statisticians' reckoning, ever carried at that depth of season by a man who finished a ten-win campaign — and from June onward he batted .305, reached at a .399 clip and slugged .663, finishing with 45 home runs, which tied for the most in the game, and 41 stolen bases: the seventh 40-40 season ever played and the first since Ohtani's of 2024 — and, counting his doubles, 30 at the least, a season's full line only Ohtani and Alfonso Soriano had ever matched.4 He led all baseball in total bases with 357, in extra-base hits with 84 and in runs scored with 119, won his second Gold Glove, and by FanGraphs' ledger was worth 10.6 wins above a replacement man — 3.6 clear of the next name on the list, the widest daylight between first and second since Mantle over Snider in 1954.4 At 24 years and 186 days he is the fifth-youngest unanimous Most Valuable by the Elias bureau's count; his is the tenth Most Valuable prize in the Cubs’ long books, though he is but the ninth man to carry one off, Banks having done it twice — the first Cub honored since Kris Bryant in 2016, and the first ever unanimous, this for the franchise of Banks, Sandberg and Sosa.53 The National League's winner has now been unanimous four Novembers running, a thing that had never happened even twice in succession before 2023.3 "I think it's just the fact that I want to be better than I was the day before," he said. "And really, that's been all that I've needed to motivate myself with for really as long as I can remember."4

The also-rans deserve their lines in the ledger. In the American League, Junior Caminero of the Sunshine nine totaled 267 points for second — the highest finish any Rays man has managed in the club's 29 seasons, which still wait on a first Most Valuable; their prior best was a pair of sixths from Evan Longoria and one from Yandy Díaz — with Bobby Witt Jr. of the Kansas City nine third at 188.26 In the National, the man unseated was the institution itself: Ohtani, the two-time reigning winner, his two-way labors halted and his bat dimmed by injury, stood second at 264 points, with Brice Turang of the champions third at 190.46 And the week's four winners share one more distinction: with Misiorowski, Schlittler and Crow-Armstrong all short of their 26th birthdays at the season's close, this is only the second awards season — 1985 was the other, with Mattingly, Saberhagen and Gooden — in which three of the four great prizes went to men so young.5 The silver season is now fully adjourned; the game belongs to the ink and the telephone.

THE EXCHANGE DESK: LAS VEGAS ADJOURNS WITH A VERDICT OF ITS OWN — THE TRADE EXPECTS SKUBAL TO LAND AMONG THE METROPOLITANS, ONE RIVAL STEWARD KNOWING NO OTHER CLUB 'EVEN IN THE CONVERSATION,' THOUGH THE SUITORS' REGISTER RUNS SIX DEEP AND THE CUBS, WANTING FIVE STARTERS, SIT OUT

The General Managers Meetings broke camp this week, and the corridors' parting judgment concerned the winter's one great arm. The widespread expectation of the industry, as the delegates scattered homeward, is that Tarik Skubal ends the winter a Met — "I don't know who else is really even in the conversation," one National League executive said of the bidding — the Flushing club being best positioned for a man seeking a long engagement, with talk of a contract running seven years to ten.7 The reader has watched this march all week: the Mets booked their audience with the left-hander for next week, as these columns recorded Wednesday, and the Blue Jays followed a day later, joining the Dodgers — his summer renters — and the Padres among the confirmed, with the Giants and the Phillies also said to have expressed interest and at least two mystery clubs besides. The arithmetic has not moved: two Cy Youngs on the mantel, and a price expected to sail past both the $325 million that Yoshinobu Yamamoto's contract marks as the guarantee record for a pitcher and the $43.33 million annual wage that Scherzer and Verlander still share.7

The curiosity of the register is the club that is not on it. The Cubs — fresh from crowning a Most Valuable, as the columns above attest — appear unlikely to enter the bidding, by the Athletic's reporting, though ESPN's man hears they want Skubal badly; and their need is no rumor, for every one of the five starters who finished the season in the Chicago rotation is now a free agent: Imanaga, Boyd, Peterson, Holmes and Gausman, the whole shelf cleared at a stroke.7 A club with a unanimous laureate in center field and not one incumbent starting pitcher is a winter story this paper intends to follow with relish.

THE CHAMPIONS' LEDGER: MILWAUKEE MEETS THE QUESTION IT TAUGHT THE LEAGUE TO ASK — IS THE SERIES' MOST VALUABLE MAN FOR SALE? ARNOLD CALLS HIS CATCHER SPECIAL AND PROMISES NOTHING, WHILE MEGILL, KEEPER OF THE LAST SIX OUTS, COLLECTS A TESTIMONIAL FROM THE FRONT OFFICE AND AN AUDIENCE WITH METALLICA

Matt Arnold spent his week in Las Vegas fielding the question his own house invented. William Contreras, who turns 29 on Christmas Eve, enters his final season before free agency now that his 2027 option is exercised — and the Milwaukee method with men in exactly that station is a matter of public record: Corbin Burnes sold to the Orioles on the eve of 2024's spring, Devin Williams to the Yankees the following winter, Freddy Peralta to the Mets going into 2026, each a contract-year star exchanged for prospects.8 Hence the morning's question, which this paper first weighed on Tuesday: does the catcher follow the pitchers out the door, or does he follow the path of Willy Adames, the shortstop the club chose to keep for a final year and let walk for a draft pick? "I'm assuming we'll get this question a lot," the president of baseball operations allowed. "But he means a lot to our team." And further: "He's really special... You saw what he did in the postseason, how he's been able to catch 1,000 innings for three years in a row, and Silver Sluggers and All-Star appearances. I don't think we win this championship without William Contreras." The October case wants no restating — a 1.036 OPS through three rounds and the first World's Series Most Valuable honor in the franchise's books. Asked whether catchers are more like pitchers or shortstops in his calculus, Arnold gave the winter's most honest answer: "They're hard to find, that's for sure."8

The same ledger holds a second name. Trevor Megill, who turns 33 early in December, enters his last winter of arbitration off a career year — a personal-best 61 and two-thirds innings, 30 saves for a second consecutive season, and the final six outs of the World's Series — and would be coveted in his own right should Milwaukee listen.8 The front office's testimony on this point is less guarded and considerably more musical: Megill, who enters to Metallica's "The Four Horsemen" at home, went to see the band at the Sphere this week while his boss was in town for the meetings, and met them besides. "He got the last six outs of the World Series, and I just went to a Metallica concert with him, so I like him," Arnold said. "I like him a lot." The Herald submits that this is the finest piece of roster analysis the meetings produced, and notes that the champions' winter — Bauers' qualifying answer due Tuesday, the catcher's telephone ringing — is only beginning.8

THE INK DESK: THE TOMAHAWK NINE BUY BACK THE ARM THEY MAILED AWAY EIGHT YEARS SINCE — PHILLIPS TAKES THREE YEARS AND FIVE-AND-THIRTY MILLIONS TO STEADY A BULLPEN OF MANY VACANCIES

The week's late signature carries a homecoming in it. Evan Phillips and the Braves agreed Thursday afternoon on a contract of three years and $35 million — $11 million in each of the first two seasons and $13 million in 2029 — returning the right-hander to the organization that made him and then mailed him to Baltimore in the 2018 trade that fetched Kevin Gausman, four appearances into his Atlanta service.9 The years between tell a journeyman's romance: let go by the Orioles, claimed off the waiver wire by the Dodgers from the Rays in August of 2021, and transformed there into one of the game's steadiest late-innings men — a 1.14 earned-run average in 2022, 2.05 in 2023 — until his elbow gave out and took Tommy John surgery in May of 2025. The comeback season just closed argues the arm is whole: a 3.46 earned-run average over 31 appearances after a first half spent convalescing, a four-seamer averaging 96.9 mph — faster than he threw in either of his great Dodger years — and a strikeout rate of 31.1 percent, near his best.9

Atlanta's need is as plain as the money. Raisel Iglesias is a free agent; Didier Fuentes, among the game's best relievers this past year, is to be stretched out as a starter in the spring, his role settled afterward; and Robert Suarez returned only in the season's final week from three months lost to a right elbow ailment. Phillips thus joins a late-innings corps being rebuilt on the fly — Suarez, Dylan Lee, the postseason revelation Ray Kerr, perhaps Iglesias again if the market returns him — and the Herald observes that the prospect Atlanta let go for nothing much in 2018 has come home at three years and $35 million — the market’s own interest, compounded over eight winters.9

THE OUTFIELD MARKET: THE BROTHERLY LOVE NINE ENTER THE SUIT FOR SATO, THE YOUNGEST BAT IN A MARKET OF OLD ONES, WHILE AT SEATTLE DIPOTO ALLOWS THAT THE PLAN HE ONCE CALLED 'Z' IS NOW MERELY EXPENSIVE

Philadelphia's outfield problem has acquired a Japanese answer. The Phillies have interest in Teruaki Sato — joining the Yankees, Mets, Dodgers and Padres in the suit for the slugger whose crossing of the Far Pacific these columns noted Tuesday — and the logic is generational arithmetic.10 Dave Dombrowski said plainly at the meetings that his club must find an outfielder before Opening Day, and as plainly that "I'm not necessarily looking for our club to continue to get older": Seiya Suzuki and Randy Arozarena, the market's two best outfield bats, are 32 and nearly so, with the projection houses placing each at roughly four years and $90 million to $108 million. Sato is 27 — younger than Bryson Stott, younger than Brandon Marsh — the Most Valuable of Japan's league in 2025 and its Triple Crown man in 2026, and is projected at five years and anywhere from $80 million to $115 million.10 The caveats are real: he swings freely and strikes out plenty, bats left-handed atop a lineup already listing that way with Harper and Schwarber, and fields indifferently enough that Philadelphia would post him in right rather than at third base. And there is history to overcome — the Phillies have courted the great Japanese free agents for years and never once been chosen, Ohtani and Yamamoto, by the local accounting, having had no interest at all.10

On the Puget Sound, meanwhile, the unthinkable has been repriced. Jerry Dipoto, who a few winters ago called trading from his starting pitching "Plan Z," told the meetings that clubs are already calling about his rotation and that he will listen: "It'll take a lot for us to move one... But if they can make us or allow us access to a hitter we otherwise wouldn't be able to access, then we have to be open."11 The inventory explains the confidence — "We're eight deep, in my mind," he said, counting the established five of Gilbert, Kirby, Woo, Miller and Hancock, plus the rookie Kade Anderson, who debuted three weeks after the Castillo sale, the ascending Ryan Sloan and the returning Logan Evans, every man of them homegrown and all but Gilbert under club control past next season. Kirby and Hancock are reckoned the likeliest to be had.11 The object of any such commerce is the same one Wednesday's columns named when the club bade farewell to its shortstop: a bat, preferably right-handed, for a lineup that lists to port. The Herald notes that "Plan Z" has quietly become "Plan: for the right price," which is how all alphabets end in November.

Friday the thirteenth, and the desk notes that the flannel-wearing men of the old game, who would not step on a foul line or lend a fellow their bat, somehow played this date every year without the sky falling; the Herald publishes accordingly, and without a rabbit's foot. The silver season is now complete — rookies Monday, managers Tuesday, pitchers Wednesday, and the Most Valuable pair last night, every prize of the writers' week bestowed and four of them without a single contrary ballot, as the columns above attest. The forward ledger was ruled open before a word was written, per the house custom, and it obliges the masthead to a small correction: the camps' reporting dates — pitchers and catchers, the first rung of winter's ladder — are still to be posted, so the paper counts instead to the first rung with a date on it, the spring exhibition slate of Friday, the 19th of February, 98 mornings from this one, with Opening Night to follow 131 mornings off, on Wednesday, the 24th of March.1 The 17th keeps its double appointment four mornings hence — qualifying answers and silver bats together — and the collective agreement has 18 mornings left to live, a figure the week's dealings at Las Vegas never once forgot. Until Saturday's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.
